sources.news_title: Dem Senate nominee admits 'I take responsibility' after police report alleges he broke down door, punched man
sources.text:
Maine Democratic Senate nominee Troy Jackson acknowledged to Fox News Digital that he got into a fight with another man nearly four decades ago, and Senate Republicans reacted to a newly surfaced police report detailing the violent confrontation.
"Nearly 40 years ago, when I was 19 years old, I got into a fight with another man. I took responsibility for it then, and I take responsibility for it now," Jackson told Fox News Digital.
"But let me be clear: I have never been violent with my partner Lana, or any other woman," Jackson added. "This happened nearly four decades ago, and I assure Mainers this incident in no way reflects the man I am today or the life I’ve led in the years since."
The National Republican Senatorial Committee (NRSC) is calling on Democrats to condemn Jackson over the report as he campaigns to unseat Republican Sen. Susan Collins in a race that could help determine control of the Senate.
"Disgusting and inexcusable," the NRSC wrote in a post on X. "Troy Jackson is violent, unhinged, and has no place in the Senate."
The NRSC also tagged a handful of Senate Democrats in posts specifically mentioning the 1988 incident, including Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I.; Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y.; Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y.; Chris Murphy, D-Conn.; Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz.; and Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass.
The NRSC also tagged Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt.; former North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper; and former Sen. Sherrod Brown, D-Ohio.
The Bangor Daily News first obtained and reported on the 1988 Fort Kent Police Department report, which the outlet said describes Jackson breaking down a door and punching a man at a Fort Kent home.
According to the newspaper's account of the police report and a handwritten witness statement, Jackson went to the home shortly before 2 a.m. March 12, 1988. After an occupant told him to leave, Jackson allegedly "kicked the door in."
Jackson then allegedly grabbed the man by the throat and swung at him, striking his glasses and cutting his face, according to the BDN's account of the records. The witness said Jackson warned the man to "stay away from Lana Pelletier or else."
The police report also notes Pelletier, Jackson's longtime partner, told an officer that Jackson had pushed her after the confrontation and that she planned to seek "cease harassment papers," according to the BDN.
Pelletier disputed that account in a statement to Fox News Digital.
"I do not remember making the statements attributed to me, and they are not accurate. This is the first time I have seen this report from 40 years ago," Pelletier said. "Troy and I have built a life and family together, and I know the person he has been through the decades since, both as a caring partner and father."
The BDN reported that it found no record Pelletier ever sought such an order.
A surviving court summary shows Jackson entered into an agreement to pay the man $50 to resolve the case, according to the BDN. The newspaper reported that the underlying court file has since been destroyed under the state's records-retention schedule.
The BDN also reported that its background check found Jackson does not have a criminal record and that the 1988 case was the only criminal case it located involving him.
Fox News Digital has made multiple attempts to independently obtain the underlying records and contacted the Fort Kent Police Department and District Court seeking the original police report. Fox News Digital additionally submitted a request through Maine's state criminal background check system, finding no viewable corresponding results.
The Fort Kent Police Department responded to Fox News Digital's request Thursday afternoon, saying the town has "sought advice from its attorneys as to whether the documents can be released."
The controversy comes shortly after Jackson secured the Democratic nomination to challenge Collins following the collapse of Graham Platner's ill-fated campaign.

sources.news_title: Reports: Maine Senate Candidate Troy Jackson Has Alleged History of Rage-Fueled Aggression Towards Women › American Greatness
sources.text:
Troy Jackson, the Democrat nominee for U.S. Senate in Maine, allegedly has a history of violent, rage-fueled aggression toward women, according to recent media reports highlighting his past blow-ups and temper tantrums.
Jackson secured the nomination at a special convention on July 25, after former Democrat nominee Graham Platner was forced to withdraw from the race due to multiple personal scandals.
According to recent reports, his replacement allegedly got physically violent with his longtime “partner” and second cousin Lana Pelletier during a fiery altercation decades ago. More recently, Jackson reportedly led the State Senate with an explosive and volatile temper, routinely yelling and cursing at female lawmakers.
Banger News Daily on Tuesday detailed a violent incident involving Jackson, Pelletier and another man in 1988, when Jackson was 19-years-old.
According to the police report, Pelletier told officers that Jackson “pushed her around” after he broke down a door and punched an apparent romantic rival at a Fort Kent home.
Just before 2 a.m. on March 12, 1988, Jackson went to a home on Market Street in Fort Kent. When he knocked on the door, one occupant told him to go away, according to the police report. Jackson refused, and that’s when he “kicked the door in,” the victim’s handwritten statement to police said.
A friend of Jackson’s who was there tried to hold him back but could not, the victim’s statement said. Jackson then went after the man, grabbed him by the throat and swung at him, hitting his glasses and cutting the man’s face, the report and victim statement said.
The victim grabbed Jackson and held him by one arm and his throat until one of Jackson’s friends got between the two men, the victim said. Jackson told the man to “stay away from Lana Pelletier or else,” the victim’s statement said.
Pelletier, who is called Jackson’s ex-girlfriend in the police report, allegedly told the responding officer that Jackson pushed her following the assault and that she planned to go to court to get “cease harassment papers” against him. But there is no record of Pelletier ever doing so, and she denied telling police those things in a statement released by Jackson’s campaign.
According to a court summary of the case, Jackson entered into an agreement to pay the man he assaulted $50. A May 1988 edition of Banger News Daily shows that he was charged with assault and paid the fine.
Pelletier told BND that the police report was “not accurate.”
“I do not remember making the statements attributed to me, and they are not accurate. This is the first time I have seen this report from 40 years ago,” she said. “Troy and I have built a life and family together, and I know the person he has been through the decades since, both as a caring partner and father.”
In a statement, Jackson did not deny assaulting the man, but insisted he had never been violent with Pelletier.
“Nearly [40] years ago, when I was 19 years old, I got into a fight with another man, he said. I took responsibility for it then, and I take responsibility for it now,” Jackson said in a statement. “But let me be clear: I have never been violent with my partner Lana, or any other woman. This happened nearly four decades ago, and I assure Mainers this incident in no way reflects the man I am today or the life I’ve led in the years since.”
Jackson is not legally married to Pelletier, although the couple has been together for decades and share two adult sons. While the Democrat has occasionally referred to Pelletier as his “wife” in past official bios, his current campaign materials and public records identify her as his “partner.” Jackson and Pelletier are reportedly second cousins, sharing the same great-grandparents.
The Washington Post recently reported that Jackson was known to be very aggressive with female lawmakers during the six years he presided over Maine’s Senate, writing that “until he left office in 2024, his temper was a feature of his leadership, and one that Democratic lawmakers discussed among themselves as a problem and even raised with the governor.”
According to the Post, people working in Maine politics characterized Jackson’s behavior as “bullying,” because “he was the most powerful Democrat in the Senate.”
One witness told the Post they were “nervous” to be in the same room as Jackson.
“It was very aggressive,” the person said. “It’s one thing to be screaming when you’re just mad about the world or sad about the world. But his screaming felt like intentional intimidation. So you would feel like then, what else is he going to do?”
During a meeting with Rachel Talbot Ross (D.), the speaker of Maine’s State House, Jackson allegedly cursed and shouted at her until she kicked him out of her office.
Another female lawmaker said he was “too emotional to be in politics.”
In 2021, Jackson allegedly threw a water bottle at then-state Sen. Heather Sanborn (D.) during an explosive confrontation that has become the stuff of legend in Maine politics.
Jackson and Sanborn were on opposing sides of a bill aimed at lowering prescription drug prices — Jackson supported the bill, while Sanborn argued it was unconstitutional and would be struck down by the courts. As one meeting wrapped up, Jackson grew angry with Sanborn and confronted her, said three people in the room that day and multiple people briefed on the fight. At one point, he threw a water bottle in anger.
“He was an inch from her nose, screaming and hollering and haranguing her,” said one of Jackson’s former legislative colleagues who was in the room.
Multiple former lawmakers told the Post that “Sanborn left the Senate that day and did not return for several days.”
“It was pretty intense,” the former colleague said. “I haven’t seen anything like that before or since.”
Jackson’s campaign adviser acknowledged that the candidate did throw a plastic water bottle but denied that he had targeted anyone.
Jackson will face incumbent Republican Senator Susan Collins in the November 2026 election.
At the time of the Post’s story, Maine Democrats had not yet selected a replacement for Platner and were expressing fear that Jackson’s reputation with female lawmakers “could hurt him in the general election” against Collins.
The senator “has won past elections in the consistently blue state by appealing to independent and left-leaning women,” the Post noted.
In a statement, the Republican National Committee said that Jackson’s past behavior toward women is “disqualifying.”
“Troy Jackson is an angry, violent man who has revealed himself to be Platner 2.0 in every way–right down to roughing up his girlfriends,” RNC Spokesperson Kristen Cianci stated, Tuesday. “How many scandals must Mainers be forced to suffer through at the hands of Democrats? This behavior is disqualifying and Jackson should read the room and drop out just like Platner.”
Cianci told American Greatness in an email that the disturbing reports do not bode well for Jackson’s fledgling Senate campaign.
“If this is what’s being reported less than three weeks after being coronated as Graham Platner’s replacement, what more will be revealed before November?” she said.

Maine Dem Senate pick Troy Jackson attacked romantic rival, ‘pushed around’ girlfriend Lana Pelletier in 1988: police report
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Add The New York Post on Google
WASHINGTON — Democratic Maine Senate hopeful Troy Jackson assaulted another man during a late-night rampage nearly four decades ago, a newly unearthed police report shows.
The March 12, 1988, brawl was apparently over Jackson’s longtime love Lana Pelletier, whom records indicate is also his second cousin and with whom the Democratic nominee shares two adult children.
The police report, first reported by the Bangor Daily News, indicates Pelletier told cops at the time that Jackson “pushed her around,” a statement she now denies making.
Jackson, then 19, had gone to a home in the town of Fort Kent, located on the Canadian border, at around 2 a.m. on the night in question, according to the report.
After the occupant of the house told Jackson to go away, the report says the future state lawmaker “kicked the door in” and grabbed his rival by the throat before punching him in the face, causing the victim’s glasses to leave a cut.
An enraged Jackson then told the unidentified man to “stay away from Lana Pelletier or else.” After the victim latched on to Jackson’s arm, a friend broke up the combatants.
The police report described Pelletier as Jackson’s ex-girlfriend, who claimed that he shoved her after the fight and that she intended to pursue a “cease harassment” order against him.
There is no indication that Pelletier ever sought the order and she has disavowed the police account of that night.
“I do not remember making the statements attributed to me, and they are not accurate. This is the first time I have seen this report from 40 years ago,” Pelletier told The Post in a statement.
“Troy and I have built a life and family together, and I know the person he has been through the decades since, both as a caring partner and father.”
The 1988 brawl is the only criminal case tied back to Jackson, and the court file has since been destroyed, according to the Bangor Daily News. However, there are indications that he paid $50 to resolve the issue.

“Nearly forty years ago, when I was 19 years old, I got into a fight with another man. I took responsibility for it then, and I take responsibility for it now,” Jackson told The Post in a statement.
“But let me be clear: I have never been violent with my partner Lana, or any other woman. This happened nearly four decades ago, and I assure Mainers this incident in no way reflects the man I am today or the life I’ve led in the years since.”
Jackson, 58, was nominated by Maine Democrats to face Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) last month after their initial nominee, Graham Platner, dropped out following rape accusations from a former girlfriend.
The Democrat has a reputation for having a hair-trigger temper and previously faced accusations that he chucked a water bottle at a female state Senate colleague during a fiery argument.
Jackson’s campaign acknowledged the dispute, but claimed he did not target the woman with the bottle.
A fifth-generation logger, Jackson spent a total of 20 years in the Maine Senate, the last six as president of the chamber.

Allagash Man Says He Witnessed Troy Jackson Strike Longtime Partner, Adding New Allegation After 1988 Police Report Surfaces
sources.text:
An Allagash man who has known Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Troy Jackson for decades says he personally witnessed Jackson strike his longtime partner, Lana Pelletier, in an incident outside a St. Francis retail store years ago, an allegation that comes as Jackson faces renewed scrutiny over a separate 1988 assault documented in a police report.
Kim McBreairty of Allagash recently sat down with The Maine Wire for an interview in northern Aroostook County, where Jackson has built much of his political identity around his roots as a logger and working-class advocate.
During the interview, McBreairty described an encounter he said he witnessed outside a small pub in neighboring St. Francis. McBreairty could not recall the exact year of the alleged incident, but said he remembers clearly what he saw.
According to McBreairty, the establishment had once been a general store before its owner converted the basement into a private pub frequented by locals on weekends.
McBreairty said he was approaching the entrance one evening when he saw Jackson standing outside with Pelletier, Jackson’s longtime partner, second cousin and the mother of his two children.
What happened next, McBreairty said, caught him completely by surprise.
“He just open-hand slapped her beside the head,” McBreairty told The Maine Wire.
McBreairty said the force of the alleged blow caused Pelletier’s head to move and her hair to fly before she turned and began walking toward the vehicle the couple had arrived in.
“Her head tilted a little bit and her hair flew,” McBreairty recalled. “She turned and started towards whatever vehicle they had.”
McBreairty said he did not hear an argument or shouting before the alleged incident and therefore could not say what, if anything, preceded it.
Asked specifically whether he saw Jackson use a closed fist or an open hand, McBreairty was unequivocal.
“Open hand,” he said. “Just whacked her.”
McBreairty said Jackson then followed Pelletier toward the vehicle. Neither Jackson nor Pelletier entered the pub that evening, according to his account.
The Maine Wire has not independently corroborated McBreairty’s account of the alleged incident. His allegation is separate from a 1988 incident reported Wednesday by the Bangor Daily News involving Jackson and Pelletier.
The BDN reported Wednesday that a police report from 1988 shows Jackson, then 19, broke down a door and punched another man at a Fort Kent residence. According to the newspaper, Jackson does not dispute assaulting the man and the misdemeanor case was ultimately resolved with a fine.
But the nearly four-decade-old police report contained another allegation.
According to the BDN, Pelletier told the responding officer at the time that Jackson had “pushed her around” following the confrontation and that she intended to seek cease-harassment papers against him. The newspaper reported that it found no record showing Pelletier ultimately sought such an order.
Both Jackson and Pelletier now dispute that portion of the police report.
Pelletier, who has been Jackson’s partner for roughly 40 years, told the BDN through Jackson’s campaign that she does not remember making the statement attributed to her by police and denied that Jackson pushed her.
Jackson acknowledged the fight with the man but categorically denied ever committing violence against Pelletier or any other woman.
“Nearly [40] years ago, when I was 19 years old, I got into a fight with another man. I took responsibility for it then, and I take responsibility for it now,” Jackson said in a statement published by the BDN.
Jackson added that the decades-old incident does not represent the person he became.
McBreairty’s account, however, raises a separate allegation: that another northern Maine resident says he personally witnessed Jackson strike Pelletier on another occasion.
McBreairty’s allegation also comes amid broader scrutiny of Jackson’s temperament during his years in Augusta. Former colleagues have described Jackson as having a fiery temper, with national and Maine news outlets recently revisiting a 2021 confrontation at the State House involving then-state Sen. Heather Sanborn, a fellow Democrat. During a heated disagreement over legislation aimed at lowering prescription drug costs, Jackson threw a plastic water bottle in frustration. Sanborn later described the episode as upsetting, while other former lawmakers have cited Jackson’s yelling and confrontational style as a concern. Jackson has acknowledged throwing the bottle, telling The New York Times that he should not have done it and conceding that he has yelled when frustrated. His campaign, however, has disputed portrayals suggesting the bottle was thrown at Sanborn, saying it was thrown away from those in the room and struck no one. The incident has nevertheless become part of a wider debate over Jackson’s temperament as he campaigns for the U.S. Senate, with Jackson characterizing his approach as passionate and saying he has taken responsibility and apologized for past outbursts.
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/07/21/us/politics/troy-jackson-maine-senate.html
McBreairty also challenged another central piece of Jackson’s public biography during his interview with The Maine Wire: Jackson’s portrayal of himself as a fifth-generation logger.
McBreairty said he has deep family connections to Jackson’s family and disputed the generational characterization.
“I know that for a fact because his grandfather and great-grandfather were trappers because they’re my uncle and grandfather,” McBreairty said.
McBreairty acknowledged that Jackson worked around logging equipment but drew a distinction between operating machinery and working as a traditional woodsman who felled trees with a chainsaw.
He said he has asked longtime residents and logging contractors around Allagash where Jackson actually worked cutting timber and has been unable to find anyone who remembers him doing that work.
“Where did Troy ever take a chainsaw and go out and fall a tree?” McBreairty asked. “Not one tree.”
McBreairty said Jackson operated equipment, including a delimber, but argued that describing that work as traditional logging gives voters an incomplete picture.
“He didn’t run a buncher, he didn’t run a chainsaw, he ran a limber,” McBreairty said.
The criticism strikes directly at the political identity Jackson has cultivated during his career in Augusta.
Jackson represented the northernmost reaches of Maine in the Legislature and eventually rose to become president of the Maine Senate, one of the most powerful positions in state government. His political image has long emphasized his Allagash roots and connection to Maine’s logging industry.
McBreairty said that history makes Jackson’s record in the region fair game as he seeks to represent the entire state in Washington.
Standing in Allagash, McBreairty pointed to a community that has lost businesses and economic opportunities over the decades and questioned what Jackson’s rise through Augusta ultimately delivered for the people who live there.
“He has done very little for the people of Maine, let alone Allagash,” McBreairty said.
The allegations from McBreairty come at a consequential moment for Jackson, who is seeking to unseat Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins.
They also create a direct factual dispute.
Jackson has publicly stated that he has never been violent toward Pelletier or any other woman. Pelletier has likewise denied the allegation contained in the 1988 police report. McBreairty, meanwhile, is now publicly putting his name behind an allegation that he personally witnessed Jackson strike Pelletier on a separate occasion.
For voters, that leaves sharply conflicting accounts surrounding events from decades ago in the small communities of northern Aroostook County, communities where Jackson’s personal history has become inseparable from the political biography he is now presenting statewide.

Since the longtime lawmaker clinched the nomination, conservative media have scrutinized their relationship after The Maine Wire reported Pelletier is Jackson’s second cousin. Both of them have large families in the region and live in a town of just over 200 people.
“I understand Maine voters want to learn about Troy as he seeks to represent them, but personal attacks on my family are unacceptable,” Pelletier said in a statement.
This isn’t the first time questions have been raised about Jackson’s conduct since he entered the high-stakes Senate race. National media reported that Jackson threw a water bottle during a heated 2021 argument with a female colleague in the Maine Senate, an episode his campaign acknowledged while disputing that he directed the object at her.
But Jackson enjoys close relationships with some of those he has sparred with. Former Rep. Charlotte Warren, D-Hallowell, who fought with him over a bill in 2021 and then made a Facebook post saying straight, white men are “too emotional” to be in politics, introduced Jackson at last month’s Democratic state convention that crowned him as the nominee.
Pelletier’s statement pivoted to the election, echoing claims that Platner and other Democrats have made about Collins’ personal wealth, which shot into the millions after she married former lobbyist and political strategist Tom Daffron in 2012. A BDN analysis from 2020 found no direct links between Daffron’s business and official actions that were scrutinized at that time.
“In the 40 years since he made a mistake as a 19-year-old kid, Troy has grown to be a passionate advocate for Mainers and dedicated his life to making things better for our state while Susan Collins has been in Washington enriching herself at our expense,” Pelletier said.
BDN writers Benjamin Kail, Daniel O’Connor and Paula Brewer contributed to this report.
Bangor Daily News investigative reporter Sawyer Loftus may be reached at sloftus@bangordailynews.com.

sources.news_title: Troy Jackson Admits To Assault After Police Report Surfaces
sources.text:
Maine Democrats have another headache on their hands after newly surfaced police records revealed that Senate candidate Troy Jackson was involved in a violent altercation nearly 40 years ago — an incident that included him breaking down a door and punching another man.
The March 1988 incident, first reported by the Bangor Daily News, occurred when Jackson was 19 years old. According to a Fort Kent Police report and a handwritten statement from the other man, Jackson arrived at a home shortly before 2 a.m. and kicked in the door after being told to leave.
Jackson then allegedly grabbed the man by the throat and swung at him, striking his glasses and cutting his face, according to the report. The man eventually restrained Jackson until one of Jackson’s friends intervened.
The man also told police that Jackson warned him to stay away from Lana Pelletier, referring ot Jackson’s girlfriend at the time and longtime partner.
Jackson does not dispute the fight.
“Nearly forty years ago, when I was 19 years old, I got into a fight with another man. I took responsibility for it then, and I take responsibility for it now,” Jackson said in a statement. “But let me be clear: I have never been violent with my partner Lana, or any other woman.”
The surviving court record shows Jackson resolved the misdemeanor assault case by agreeing to pay the man $50. A background check conducted by the Bangor Daily News found no other criminal record associated with Jackson.
The police report also contains an allegation involving Pelletier. According to the report, Pelletier told an officer that Jackson had “pushed her around” following the altercation and that she intended to seek “cease harassment papers.”
Pelletier disputes that account.
“I do not remember making the statements attributed to me, and they are not accurate,” Pelletier said. “This is the first time I have seen this report from 40 years ago. Troy and I have built a life and family together and I know the person he has been through the decades since, both as a caring partner and father.”
Jackson and Pelletier —unmarried second cousins— have been together for roughly four decades and have two adult sons.
The revelation comes at an awkward time for Jackson, who only recently emerged as the Democratic Party’s replacement nominee in the race against Republican Sen. Susan Collins after the collapse of Graham Platner’s campaign.
Jackson has already faced questions about his temper during the current campaign.
In 2021, while serving as president of the Maine Senate, Jackson became embroiled in a heated dispute with then-state Sen. Heather Sanborn over legislation. Multiple witnesses told the New York Times that Jackson lost his temper and threw a half-empty water bottle across the room.
The witnesses said the bottle did not hit Sanborn and was not aimed at her, and Jackson later apologized. One Democratic senator who witnessed the incident described it as an “anger spell.”
Jackson acknowledged that he should not have thrown the bottle, while insisting that he was simply passionate about the issue.

sources.news_title: Bangor Daily News: Troy Jackson punched a man and pushed his partner in 1988, police report says
sources.text:
Troy Jackson punched a man and pushed his partner in 1988, police report says
Sawyer Loftus
Bangor Daily News
August 12, 2026
Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Troy Jackson’s longtime partner told an officer he “pushed her around” after Jackson broke down a door and punched a man at a Fort Kent home in 1988, according to a police report obtained exclusively by the Bangor Daily News.
Jackson, who was 19 at the time, does not dispute the assault of the man, a misdemeanor charge resolved by a fine. But Lana Pelletier, who has been in a relationship with Jackson for roughly 40 years, says she has no memory of making the statement attributed to her by police and denied he pushed her. In a statement, Jackson denied he had ever been violent with her.
“Nearly [40] years ago, when I was 19 years old, I got into a fight with another man. I took responsibility for it then, and I take responsibility for it now,” Jackson said in a statement. “But let me be clear: I have never been violent with my partner Lana, or any other woman. This happened nearly four decades ago, and I assure Mainers this incident in no way reflects the man I am today or the life I’ve led in the years since.”
The unearthing of the old case comes less than three weeks after Jackson secured the Democratic nomination in an unprecedented sprint to replace Graham Platner on the ballot in a race with five-term Republican Sen. Susan Collins that is pivotal to control of the chamber. Platner’s campaign collapsed after an ex-girlfriend’s allegation that he raped her in 2021.
Jackson, a former Maine Senate president from Allagash who is now 58, does not have a criminal record, according to a background check run by the BDN. The 1988 case was the only criminal one linked to Jackson in a search of state court records. The underlying court file has been destroyed under the judicial system’s retention schedule.
But the report at the Fort Kent Police Department and a handwritten witness statement lay out an account of that night.
Just before 2 a.m. on March 12, 1988, Jackson went to a home on Market Street in Fort Kent. When he knocked on the door, one occupant told him to go away, according to the police report. Jackson refused, and that’s when he “kicked the door in,” the victim’s handwritten statement to police said.
A friend of Jackson’s who was there tried to hold him back but could not, the victim’s statement said. Jackson then went after the man, grabbed him by the throat and swung at him, hitting his glasses and cutting the man’s face, the report and victim statement said.
The victim grabbed Jackson and held him by one arm and his throat until one of Jackson’s friends got between the two men, the victim said. Jackson told the man to “stay away from Lana Pelletier or else,” the victim’s statement said.
Pelletier, who is called Jackson’s ex-girlfriend in the police report, allegedly told the responding officer that Jackson pushed her following the assault and that she planned to go to court to get “cease harassment papers” against him…
